assessments.technical_explanation: The gitleaks generic-api-key match at line 454 of file lands on a call to judgment_view, an internal helper that filters judgment records for a character's scene payload. The line contains only variable names, keyword arguments, and a set-computed subject list; no literal key, token, or secret value is present in the supplied source. The function reads from the local charter record and produces model-prompt data, matching the project's stated purpose of assembling per-character perception slices. The scanner match is a false positive on ordinary Python source text.

assessments.technical_explanation: The JS-X-Ray 'shady-link' signal at line 1680 points to API-path string construction used by a single-player local front end. The flagged code builds relative URLs for the application's own backend endpoints (chat body station updates, chat attire and world state records), interpolating a chat identifier and a URL-encoded body name. The scheme-relative path format resembles the pattern the scanner flags as suspicious links, but these are same-origin fetch calls to the engine's local FastAPI server, matching the stated purpose of the world browser UI. No cross-origin destination, external network call, obfuscated string assembly, or credential-bearing URL is present anywhere in the supplied context.
assessments.layman_explanation: An automated scanner flagged this line as containing a suspicious link. Looking at the actual code, it is just the app talking to its own local server to save and load scene data, which is exactly what this world-editing screen is supposed to do. Nothing is sent anywhere else.
assessments.developer_action: None required. The scanner match reflects ordinary same-origin API calls that are consistent with the project's purpose.

assessments.technical_explanation: The flagged regex matches a closed set of short literal tag names with one optional literal attribute, contains no nested quantifiers, no alternation of variable-length groups under repetition, and no ambiguity that could cause catastrophic backtracking; input length is bounded by a single turn of prose. It is used with matchAll to find emphasis tags in model-generated prose, and the surrounding rendering code builds DOM nodes directly rather than using innerHTML, with the color attribute restricted to a class name from a closed vocabulary. This is a well-constructed, linear-time pattern and the rendering path it feeds is designed specifically to keep model output from becoming markup. At worst, a pathological input only slows matching linearly with text length, which is the recoverable, low-impact case.
assessments.layman_explanation: A code scanner flagged this pattern as potentially 'unsafe', but it is a simple, tightly written search for a few formatting tags like bold and italic in story text. It cannot hang the browser or let story text turn into hidden code; the surrounding code deliberately renders text safely.

observations.title: Save handler suppresses fetch errors without user feedback
observations.technical_explanation: The Raw JSON tab's save handler re-reads the current record to detect concurrent edits, and if that re-read fails the failure is swallowed and treated as if the record were unchanged. Similarly, an exception during the subsequent PUT is not caught, so the tab may not surface the failure state to the user. This is a local reliability issue only: the endpoints are same-origin, the failure mode is a confusing or lost manual edit within the user's own single-player session, and no attacker-controlled path or external data flow is involved.
observations.layman_explanation: If something goes wrong while checking or saving the raw record, the screen may stay quiet about it and the user's manual edit can be lost. This is a usability bug, not a security problem.
observations.developer_action: Distinguish a failed freshness re-read from an unchanged record, and catch and surface PUT errors so the user knows their save did not land.
